sections.h2: How an Indiana property tax lien works
sections.html:
Indiana's property tax lien is created by statute and sits on the land itself. IC 6-1.1-22-13 puts every parcel of real estate under a lien for its levied taxes, along with any penalties and costs.

It attaches on the assessment date for the tax year. A sale or transfer does not erase it. List a house with a year of tax unpaid and the lien stays on the parcel until somebody pays, so the title company deals with it when you close.

The same law ranks it above every other lien. Mortgages, judgment liens and contractor claims all come after it. It lasts ten years from May 10 of the year the taxes first became due, and that period can stretch if the county starts enforcement inside it.

sections.h2: When Indiana property tax becomes delinquent
sections.html:
An installment goes delinquent the day after it is missed. Under IC 6-1.1-22-9, a year's tax is generally split into two equal payments, due May 10 and November 10 of the following year. A weekend or holiday pushes the deadline to the next business day. The state's Department of Local Government Finance keeps a due dates page with the current schedule.

Your payment is timely if it arrives, carries a postmark, or goes out by electronic transfer on or before the deadline (IC 6-1.1-37-10). Once an installment is late, penalties start right away.

The first penalty is either 5 percent or 10 percent of the delinquent amount. The 5 percent rate applies when a real property installment is paid in full within 30 days of the due date and the owner has no earlier delinquency on that parcel. Every other late payment is charged 10 percent. Marion County describes it the same way: pay within 30 days with no back taxes and the penalty is 5 percent, and after that it is 10 percent.

Later years add more. In each following year, another 10 percent applies to unpaid tax on the day after each installment due date. Those later penalties land on the unpaid principal only, so a penalty does not compound on an earlier penalty.

Late payment situationPenalty added
Paid within 30 days, no earlier delinquency on the parcel5% of the delinquent amount
Any other late payment10% of the amount due
Still unpaid after each later installment dateAdditional 10% on unpaid principal

sections.h2: What happens when the tax stays unpaid
sections.html:
The county can eventually put the parcel into a tax sale, which is the main way a tax lien turns into a change of ownership. A taxing unit can also sue the person liable and recover the tax, penalties and collection costs, including reasonable attorney fees and court costs.

Counties take the steps in order:

  • The county auditor builds a delinquency list and a notice of sale.
  • The county treasurer and auditor ask the court for a judgment and an order of sale.
  • The property is offered at a public auction, subject to redemption.
  • The owner gets a redemption window before a buyer can ask for a tax deed.

Our Indiana tax sale page covers the auction and the redemption window in detail. This page stays on the lien and on clearing it.

sections.h2: Can you set up a payment plan on delinquent taxes?
sections.html:
Yes, the law contemplates one. IC 6-1.1-24-1.2 covers removing a property from the delinquency list and arranging to pay delinquent taxes. Each county sets its own terms, so ask your treasurer what it will take.

Marion County treats a tax sale payment plan and partial payments as separate topics on its Stop a Tax Sale page. The Treasurer's Office is at (317) 327-4444 or mytaxes@indy.gov. Behind on a plan? Call before a sale date is set.

A plan has limits if you plan to sell. The lien remains until the tax is paid in full, and a buyer's title company will still want a payoff at closing.

Unpaid state tax can also become a lien on your house, in whichever county the warrant is recorded. This one is separate from the property tax lien. After a demand notice goes unanswered for 20 days, the Department of State Revenue can issue a tax warrant, and a 10 percent collection fee is added to the unpaid tax (IC 6-8.1-8-2).

The circuit court clerk records the warrant as a judgment against the taxpayer, and that judgment gives the state a lien on the taxpayer's real and personal property interests there. A filed judgment is valid for 10 years and can be renewed for further 10 year periods.

The two liens differ in timing. The property tax lien attaches on the assessment date and ranks above every other lien. The warrant lien attaches when the clerk records the judgment, and it reaches only the county where it was recorded.

A taxpayer can ask for a release once the debt is satisfied, and the department must release a warrant issued in error. Ask your title company to run a search so any warrant shows up before you list.

A few delinquent parcels never go through the regular sale, and their owners get no redemption right. IC 6-1.1-24-1.5 lets a county, city or town executive certify a delinquent property that a court or hearing authority found vacant or abandoned. The auditor then sells it at auction, and the owner cannot redeem after the sale date.

The minimum bid on those parcels equals the property's share of the county's actual sale costs, not the full tax debt. A vacant house with years of unpaid tax is exactly what this rule targets.

  • The tax must be delinquent from the prior year's fall installment or earlier.
  • A court or hearing authority must find the property vacant or abandoned.
  • The auditor publishes the sale notice at least 30 days before the sale.

Marion County places a tax lien on homes with unpaid property taxes and sells those liens at an online auction each year. Registered bidders put down a $2,500 deposit for the regular portion of the sale.

To stop a scheduled sale, an owner pays all unpaid taxes, penalties and special assessments, solid waste and stormwater fees, and a $325 tax sale administration fee. The cutoff is 4:30 p.m. on a day shortly before the sale, and payment is limited to cash, certified check, cashier's check or money order.

Marion County Treasurer: City-County Building, 200 E. Washington St., Suite 1001, Indianapolis, IN 46204. Auditor: Suite W-125, phone 317.327.4646.

Most sellers never write a check for the lien. Closing pays it: the title agent requests a payoff from the county treasurer and sends the money from your proceeds.

Do these four things early:

  • Get the current tax bill and a payoff number with penalties included.
  • Search for a state tax warrant filed under your name.
  • Find out if the parcel sits on a delinquency list or already has a sale date.
  • With a sale date close, ask the treasurer what time payment is due and what forms of payment it takes.

Cash Home Buyers can purchase a house carrying these liens and coordinate with the title company so the unpaid tax is paid out of what you receive. A cash sale skips repairs and showings. You can ask for an offer without fixing a thing.

faqs.q: How long does a property tax lien last in Indiana?
faqs.a: Ten years from May 10 of the year the taxes first became due. If the county starts enforcement inside that period, the deadline can extend as needed to finish it.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house with a tax lien in Indiana?
faqs.a: Yes. The lien follows the property, so the unpaid tax is paid from the sale proceeds at closing. A title company confirms the payoff amount before the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Does a tax lien rank ahead of my mortgage?
faqs.a: Yes. IC 6-1.1-22-13 makes the property tax lien superior to all other liens, so it is paid before a mortgage in a forced sale.

faqs.q: What is the penalty for paying Indiana property tax late?
faqs.a: Five percent if you pay within 30 days and have no earlier delinquency on the parcel, and ten percent in any other case. Another 10 percent applies to unpaid principal after each later due date.

faqs.q: Who do I call in Indianapolis about delinquent property tax?
faqs.a: Call the Marion County Treasurer's Office at (317) 327-4444 for balances and payments. The Auditor's Office at 317.327.4646 handles tax sale questions.
